paper.title: REvolve: Reward Evolution with Large Language Models using Human Feedback
paper.source_version: arXiv v4, 2025-05-23; latest public arXiv version verified 2026-08-30. Published at ICLR 2025. Official code release v1.0.0 is commit 6ccae3c61a4915b3fb61f75947e21a8dd8232888; latest public main inspected at commit eee636b5dba141bf00cf0ff47852c2a9125dc5d2 (2026-08-24).

decision_relevance.why_admitted: REvolve directly searches executable task-reward programs while holding each task's simulator, policy algorithm, hyperparameters, and candidate budget fixed; it adds an island population, LLM mutation/crossover, human Elo fitness, and natural-language feedback, and evaluates the best policies with a fresh human cohort.
not_evidence_for: reference-motion selection, composition, playback, phase conditioning, predicates, branching, or any other oracle mechanism
safe or sandboxed execution of generated Python reward code
a turnkey public implementation of the reported human-feedback loop or paper-scale training budget
portability across controllers, optimizers, simulators, observation contracts, training budgets, or hardware
deterministic replay or an immutable execution manifest

mechanisms.name: Fixed-world reward-design contract
mechanisms.description: The reward-design problem separates world M=(S,A,T), executable reward R, policy trained on R, rollout distribution, and fitness F; the outer objective chooses R to maximize expected fitness of the resulting policy.

mechanisms.name: Island-population reward search
mechanisms.description: A database stores tuples (reward, trained policy, scalar fitness, text feedback) across I islands. Islands and parents are sampled by fitness; accepted children must meet or exceed the destination island mean; periodic migration resets weaker islands from fitter lineages; final selection takes the highest-fitness tuple.

mechanisms.name: LLM mutation and crossover of executable rewards
mechanisms.description: GPT-4 Turbo receives task text plus a subset of allowed observation/action variables and emits Python rewards expressed as a sum of named components. Mutation revises one component from one parent; crossover combines high-performing components from two parents using component traces and feedback.

mechanisms.name: Pairwise Elo plus natural-language feedback
mechanisms.description: Evaluators compare approximately 30-40 second rollout videos, with ties allowed. Pairwise outcomes become Elo fitness; selected positive and negative behavior checkboxes are converted to text and returned to the LLM for reproduction.

mechanisms.name: Train-every-candidate policy loop
mechanisms.description: Every reward candidate trains a new policy under the task's fixed inner algorithm and budget: Clipped Double DDQN in AirSim or SAC in MuJoCo. Rollouts and fitness feed the reward search; policy parameters are not the outer authoring knob.

mechanisms.name: Public research-code execution path
mechanisms.description: At the pinned latest commit, the release queries GPT-4, parses a compute_reward function, checks only argument membership and the presence of a return, executes it with Python exec, trains policies in parallel, and evaluates the main loop from velocity logs. Human Elo preprocessing remains a separate script rather than an integrated main-loop evaluator.

failure_modes.name: Compute-heavy, low-seed search
failure_modes.description: Every reward trains a fresh policy. One sixteen-policy generation takes about 50 hours in AirSim or 24 hours in MuJoCo on sixteen A100s, while main results use only two random seeds; selection and comparisons can therefore remain sensitive to RL variance.

failure_modes.name: Sparse automatic feedback limits search
failure_modes.description: The authors report that velocity-only Humanoid feedback and steps-to-success Adroit feedback are less informative than detailed human feedback; human-guided variants outperform automatic counterparts and gains stabilize around generation five.

failure_modes.name: Limited generalization and no real-world test
failure_modes.description: AirSim performance drops in the denser-traffic unseen environment, partly attributed by the authors to missed oncoming cars in the visual module. No analogous MuJoCo variants were available, and real-world applicability is left as future work.

failure_modes.name: Closed LLM dependence and no optimality guarantee
failure_modes.description: The method depends on closed-source GPT-4; the authors state the highest-fitness database policy is not necessarily optimal.

failure_modes.name: Adroit observation-contract contradiction
failure_modes.description: Main Table 1 reports a 39-dimensional Adroit observation, while Appendix A.1.3 reports 97 dimensions. The exact environment interface cannot be reconstructed from the paper without resolving this contradiction.

failure_modes.name: Paper-to-code protocol gap
failure_modes.description: The latest public defaults use fifteen candidates, four islands, and one thousand policy steps rather than the paper's sixteen candidates, thirteen islands, and five million MuJoCo steps. The public main loop uses velocity fitness, while human Elo processing is a separate script that imports a symbol absent from the pinned database module.

failure_modes.name: Unsandboxed generated Python
failure_modes.description: The public release passes LLM-generated function text to Python exec after checking only exposed argument names and the presence of a return. It does not establish side-effect freedom, resource bounds, or an execution sandbox.

failure_modes.name: Released Elo scores depend on row order and pool
failure_modes.description: The released script updates Elo sequentially in CSV row order and then min-max normalizes ratings over the current comparison pool. Exact fitness values therefore depend on comparison order and pool composition, even though ranking may be more stable.

evaluation.name: Fresh-cohort human ranking
evaluation.description: A cohort disjoint from training compared rollouts from the best policies. REvolve outranked Eureka in autonomous driving (1575 vs 1499), Humanoid (1586 vs 1557), and Adroit (1594 vs 1522); only human driving outranked REvolve in autonomous driving.

evaluation.name: Fixed-budget task-fitness comparison
evaluation.description: Across two seeds, the best policy per generation is evaluated with task-specific fitness. The paper reports REvolve above Eureka, automatic variants, and expert rewards across all three tasks, with gains stabilizing around generation five.

evaluation.name: Mutation/crossover ablation
evaluation.description: In autonomous driving over seven generations, the paper reports combined mutation and crossover above crossover-only, which is above mutation-only; the figure does not tabulate exact endpoint values.

evaluation.name: Unseen-AirSim reward transfer
evaluation.description: Policies were retrained from scratch with the best reward in two unseen AirSim environments. REvolve exceeded Eureka and expert rewards in both, but performance was substantially lower in the denser-traffic second environment.

evidence.locator: Header and submission history; arXiv v4 dated 23 May 2025
evidence.claim: The exact analyzed paper is arXiv 2406.01309v4 with the listed title and five authors; the arXiv record marks it published at ICLR 2025.
The paper appears in the International Conference on Learning Representations 2025 proceedings.
The reward-design problem separates M=(S,A,T), candidate reward R, the policy trained with R, rollout distribution, and fitness F, and optimizes expected policy fitness over R.

REvolve stores reward-policy-fitness-feedback tuples in islands, trains a policy for each child, accepts fitness at least equal to the island mean, and returns the highest-fitness tuple while disclaiming policy optimality.
The method samples islands and parents by fitness, uses one parent for mutation and two for crossover, asks GPT-4 to revise or combine reward components, and periodically migrates individuals.
Evaluators compare approximately 30-40 second rollout videos with ties allowed; Elo yields scalar fitness and selected positive/negative behavior checkboxes yield natural-language feedback for GPT-4.

Experiments cover AirSim autonomous driving and MuJoCo Humanoid and Adroit; GPT-4 Turbo 1106-preview receives a subset of observation/action variables and emits a sum of self-chosen reward components.

The reported search uses seven generations, sixteen candidates per generation, thirteen islands, mutation probability 0.5, 500,000 AirSim or 5,000,000 MuJoCo steps per candidate, sixteen 40GB A100s, about 50 or 24 hours per generation, and two seeds; Table 1 states a 39-D Adroit observation.

The paper reports REvolve above all non-human baselines across three tasks, notes richer human feedback beats sparse automatic feedback, and uses a fresh evaluator cohort for final Elo scores of 1575, 1586, and 1594 for REvolve versus 1499, 1557, and 1522 for Eureka.

Combined mutation and crossover outperform either alone in autonomous driving; retraining from the best reward in two unseen AirSim environments beats Eureka and expert rewards, with lower generalization in denser traffic.
The authors identify expensive multi-policy training and closed-source GPT-4 dependence as limitations.
Elo initializes every individual at 1500, uses update factor 32 and win/tie/loss values 1, 0.5, and 0, and recomputes ratings using comparisons within and across generations.
The appendix specifies AirSim DDQN and SB3 SAC interfaces and hyperparameters; it describes the Adroit observation as 97-D, contradicting the 39-D main-table value.

The study used ten evaluators per generation and twenty pairs per evaluator; the authors estimate 1,400 pair samples over seven generations and database growth of about 2.5GB per generation, 17.5GB total.

Prompts require executable Python returning total reward plus component diagnostics, constrain inputs to exposed environment variables, and define mutation/crossover using component histories and human feedback.
